i: This Book takes its name from queen Esther, whose history is here recorded. The general opinion of almost all commentators on the Holy Scriptures makes Mordecai the writer of it: which also may be collected below from chap. 9 ver. 20.

a.1: King Ahasuerus makes a great feast. Queen Vashti being sent for refuses to come: for which disobedience she is deposed.
a.2: Esther is advanced to be queen. Mordecai detects a plot against the king.
a.3: Haman, advanced by the king, is offended at Mordecai, and therefore procures the king's decree to destroy the whole nation of the Jews.
a.4: Mordecai desires Esther to petition the king for the Jews. They join in fasting and prayer.
a.5: Esther is graciously received: she invites the king and Haman to dinner, Haman prepares a gibbet for Mordecai.
a.6: The king hearing of the good service done him by Mordecai, commands Haman to honour him next to the king, which he performs.
a.7: Esther's petition for herself and her people: Haman is hanged upon the gibbet he had prepared for Mordecai.
a.8: Mordecai is advanced: Haman's letters are reversed.
a.9: The Jews kill their enemies that would have killed them. The days of Phurim are appointed to be kept holy.
a.11: The dream of Mordecai, which in the ancient Greek and Latin Bibles was into the beginning of the book, but was detached by St. Jerome, and put in this place.
a.12: Mordecai detects the conspiracy of the two eunuchs.
a.13: A copy of a letter sent by Haman to destroy the Jews. Mordecai's prayer for the people.
a.14: The prayer of Esther for herself and her people.
a.15: Esther comes into the king's presence: she is terrified, but God turns his heart.
a.16: A copy of the king's letter in favour of the Jews.

6:3: No reward at all... He received some presents from the king, chap. 12.5; but these were so inconsiderable in the opinion of the courtiers, that they esteemed them as nothing at all.
9:1: To revenge, etc... The Jews on this occasion, by authority from the king, were made executioners of the public justice, for punishing by death a crime worthy of death, viz., a malicious conspiracy for extirpating their whole nation.
10:4: Then Mordecai, etc... Here St. Jerome advertises the reader, that what follows is not in the Hebrew, but is found in the septuagint Greek edition, which the seventy-two interpreters translated out of the Hebrew, or added by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
10:5: A dream... This dream was prophetical and extraordinary: otherwise the general rule is not to observe dreams.
16:1: From India to Ethiopia... That is, who reigns from India to Ethiopia.
